paper_title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: An agent harness is the software infrastructure that manages interactions between large language model (LLM) and its environment (Grace et al., 2026). Recent work on recursive self-improvement (RSI) (Zhang et al., 2026) uses past execution trajectories to diagnose problems and guide harness updates that improve performance on future tasks (Suzgun et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026a). However, these methods often pursue performance gains through more extensive exploration and stronger verification (Lin et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026a). These efforts improve performance, but often at the cost of higher token consumption and increased latency. This trade-off is less appealing in practical deployment, where the execution cost and latency also matter. We therefore ask: Can recursive harness self-improvement deliver better performance at lower execution cost? Toward this goal, we introduce HARNESSPRO, label-free method for recursive harness selfimprovement that uses both performance and cost metrics to guide harness updates and candidate selection. It orchestrates several specialized agents to turn execution feedback into successive harness updates. trajectory analyzer examines repeated rollouts to identify failures and avoidable overhead. Guided by different performance-cost priorities, planner turns these diagnoses into harness improvement plans, which an editor implements as executable harness candidates. testsynthesis agent provides fixed tests for evaluating the candidates without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Candidates that underperform the initial harness or are Pareto-dominated are discarded. To accommodate different budgets, we then use normalized weighted squared-distance selection (Marler & Arora, 2004) to retain representative harnesses for cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) modes. The selected harnesses then enter the next epoch, where further updates pursue different performance-cost priorities.

sections.title: Under review
sections.content: We evaluate HARNESSPRO on Terminal-Bench 2 (The Terminal-Bench Team, 2025), SWE-Bench Pro (Deng et al., 2026), and ProgramBench (Yang et al., 2026a), using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. With both backbone models, HARNESSPRO improves task performance while reducing execution cost. For example, on Terminal-Bench 2 with GPT-5.5 and Codex, the heavy mode of HARNESSPRO outperforms RHO (Pan et al., 2026a) in pass rate by 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean cost per task by 33.9%. For more cost-sensitive deployments, the medium mode delivers performance comparable to RHO at substantially lower execution cost. An analysis of the evolved harnesses shows that HARNESSPRO does not improve agents simply by compressing context or increasing reasoning effort. The evolved harnesses dynamically allocate reasoning effort and tool budgets based on task descriptions, while runtime hooks steer execution from exploration toward convergence based on the assigned budgets. They also adopt tool-output compression like RTK (Szymkowiak, 2026) and streamline instructions to reduce redundant prompt content, while retaining necessary context and final verification. Together, these mechanisms curb avoidable overhead while preserving the reasoning and verification needed for task success, thereby advancing the performance-cost Pareto frontier. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce HARNESSPRO, multi-agent framework that simultaneously optimizes performance and cost by analyzing execution trajectories and recursively improving harnesses. We assess candidate artifacts with fixed LLM-generated tests rather than direct LLM judgments, improving failure detection without access to official tests. Across three benchmarks, HARNESSPRO improves performance while reducing cost and latency, yielding series of harnesses with different performance-cost trade-offs.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Agent and harness optimization. Agent optimization has expanded from prompts and predefined workflows to the executable harness surrounding model. AFlow searches graphs of modelinvoking operators using execution feedback (Zhang et al., 2025). More recent systems directly modify harness components: agentic harness engineering makes edits traceable (Lin et al., 2026), HarnessFix diagnoses failures before applying repairs (Chen et al., 2026a), and HarnessX composes harnesses from typed primitives using trajectory evidence (Chen et al., 2026b). RHO uses LLMs to evaluate and compare execution trajectories without ground-truth labels, guiding harness evolution toward higher task success (Pan et al., 2026a). In contrast, our method, HARNESSPRO, optimizes both task success rate and monetary cost. Rather than returning single harness, it produces set of harnesses with different performance-cost trade-offs, organized into lite, medium, and heavy tiers. Component optimization and inference-time budget allocation. Some methods focus on specific components, such as skills or memory (Pan et al., 2026b). SkillOpt optimizes skill documents (Yang et al., 2026b), while SkillMOO and FRAMES incorporate cost or regression constraints into skill evolution (Gong et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026). Dynamic Cheatsheet and ReasoningBank retain reusable strategies from past experience (Suzgun et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2026), while Sleep-time Compute builds reusable memory by reasoning over context before query arrives (Lin et al., 2025). MemoryCPT jointly optimizes memory construction, retrieval, and summarization (Lei et al., 2026). Other work addresses budget allocation at inference time: BATS learns budget-aware policy for allocating model tokens and external tool calls (Liu et al., 2025), while COMPAS jointly selects models, prompts, and decoding settings according to task difficulty (Gong et al., 2026b). HARNESSPRO instead uses past trajectories to evolve the entire harness, including instructions, skills, tools, hooks, and verification rules. Table 1 summarizes how HARNESSPRO differs from prior work.

sections.title: 4.1 OVERVIEW
sections.content: To keep trajectory collection and analysis manageable, we begin by selecting training coreset Dtrain. Following RHO (Pan et al., 2026a), we use the Determinantal Point Process (DPP) kernel (Kulesza & Taskar, 2012) to balance task difficulty and diversity (Appendix A.1). Starting from an executable harness h0, we maintain candidate set At of harnesses at epoch t, initialized as A0 = {h0}. In each epoch, HARNESSPRO employs multi-agent framework to analyze trajectories of these candidate harnesses on the coreset Dtrain to identify task failures, unproductive exploration, and redundant computation. The framework then plans and implements harness modifications to address these issues, producing new executable candidate harnesses as described in Section 4.2. We evolve harnesses in label-free setting, without access to ground-truth solutions, official test cases, or graders. Instead of using an LLM to assess and compare trajectories directly, as in RHO (Pan et al., 2026a), we use it to generate tests from task descriptions and trajectories produced by the initial harness. In each epoch, we evaluate candidate harnesses on the validation set using the generated tests, measuring pass rate and execution cost. After discarding candidates that fall below the performance floor or are Pareto-dominated, we use normalized weighted squared-distance selection to retain representatives for cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) modes. The selected harnesses form the candidate set for the next epoch. This process repeats until the epoch limit is reached, after which we fix the harnesses and evaluate them on the test set. Algorithm 1 summarizes the full procedure.

sections.title: 5.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Data and implementation. We evaluate HARNESSPRO on Terminal-Bench 2 (The TerminalBench Team, 2025), SWE-Bench Pro (Deng et al., 2026), and ProgramBench (Yang et al., 2026a), covering terminal tasks, repository-level issue resolution, and program reconstruction. Following the dataset splitting protocol of RHO (Pan et al., 2026a), we hold out 59, 100, and 100 tasks, respectively, for testing. From the remaining tasks in each benchmark, we select 10-task training set Dtrain using the DPP-based coreset selection method (Kulesza & Taskar, 2012) described in Section 4.1. The remaining tasks form the validation set. We pair GPT-5.5 with Codex 0.147.0 and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code 2.1.231. Each candidate harness produces = 3 rollouts per training task in each epoch. Evolution runs for three epochs on Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, and four on ProgramBench, retaining up to three harnesses after each epoch. All methods use the same data splits and grading settings. Further implementation details are in Appendix A. Baselines. We compare HARNESSPRO against several strong harness optimization methods. The original Codex or Claude Code harness is Vanilla, the starting point for optimization. Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al., 2026) maintains reusable strategies and code snippets, ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2026) retrieves strategies distilled from past trajectories, and Sleep-time Compute (Lin et al., 2025) prepares reusable memory before new tasks. RHO (Pan et al., 2026a) revises harness components through trajectory analysis and selects candidates using LLM self-preference. To separate the effects of cost-aware and recursive optimization, we include two RHO variants. Balance changes only RHOs optimization instruction, asking for better task performance at lower cost. RHO+Iteration runs Balance for the same number of epochs as HARNESSPRO. Each subsequent epoch starts from the harness selected in the preceding epoch by the best-of-N procedure of RHO. Evaluation metrics. On Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, task passes only if all its official tests pass. For ProgramBench, we follow its official evaluation protocol (Yang et al., 2026a) and report pass rate as the macro-average of the fraction of test cases passed for each task. We also report mean cost C(h) and latency L(h). For HARNESSPRO, all metrics are given as mean sample standard deviation over three runs on Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, and two on ProgramBench. The token prices used to calculate cost are listed in Table 4 in the appendix.

sections.title: 5.2 MAIN RESULTS
sections.content: Table 2 compares HARNESSPRO with several baseline methods across three benchmarks. With GPT-5.5 and Codex, RHO improves performance over Vanilla on all three benchmarks, but also increases execution cost. On SWE-Bench Pro, for example, its mean cost per task rises by 42.6%, from $1.88 to $2.68. In contrast, the heavy mode of HARNESSPRO achieves the highest pass rate across all three benchmarks at lower cost than RHO. On Terminal-Bench 2, the heavy mode of HARNESSPRO reaches mean pass rate of 80.8% across three runs, 4.5 percentage points above RHO, with 33.9% lower mean cost. The advantage extends to ProgramBench, where its 69.6% pass rate exceeds RHOs 68.8% at 17.8% lower mean cost ($2.95 vs. $3.59). These results show that better task performance need not come at higher execution cost. For the medium mode, we retain strong task performance while reducing cost further. On SWE-Bench Pro, it achieves 79.0% pass rate compared with RHOs 80.0%, while reducing the average cost per task by 53.0%, from $2.68 to $1.26. The lite mode lowers cost further, outperforming Vanilla on all three benchmarks while spending 17.757.4% less, making it an economical choice for deployment under strict budget constraints. Even with comparable iteration budgets, HARNESSPRO achieves better performance cost trade-off than RHO+Iteration. Our medium mode matches the performance of RHO+Iteration on Terminal-Bench 2 at 31.7% lower cost. Moreover, on ProgramBench, our heavy mode raises pass rate by 1.3 percentage points while lowering mean cost by 5.8%. The results with GLM-5.2 and Claude Code follow similar pattern: the heavy mode of HARNESSPRO surpasses RHO on all three benchmarks at lower cost, while the medium and lite modes outperform Vanilla in pass rate, often at substantially lower cost. Moreover, although latency is not an objective, cost optimization yields faster task completion in most cases. For example, on SWE-Bench Pro, our heavy mode reduces mean latency from RHOs 520 to 412 seconds.

sections.title: 5.3 ANALYSIS OF EVOLVED HARNESSES
sections.content: To understand how HARNESSPRO improves the performance-cost trade-off, we inspect its evolved harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, they select an execution profile from each task description. Each profile specifies reasoning effort level and tool-call budget. The lite, medium, and heavy modes use different rubrics for profile selection. Runtime hooks enforce the selected budget. For example, on Terminal-Bench 2, when HARNESSPRO-Medium selects the standard profile, the hooks remind the agent to produce parallel tool calls and avoid redundant checks after 14 tool calls, focus on completing and verifying the task after 26, and block further calls after 44. The reminders are appended to tool results, preserving the prompt prefix for cache reuse. Alongside these dynamic mechanisms, the evolved harnesses also reduce static context redundancy. On Terminal-Bench 2, for instance, tool-output compression like RTK (Szymkowiak, 2026) folds repeated logs and condenses long outputs, while streamlined developer instructions reduce redundant input. This combination curbs recurring prompt overhead and limits the context growth caused by verbose tool feedback, thereby reducing execution cost and latency. Implementation details of these harnesses are in Appendix D.1.

sections.title: 5.4 EVOLUTION DYNAMICS
sections.content: Figure 4 tracks test-set performance and cost across epochs. Across all three benchmarks, HARNESSPRO advances the performance-cost Pareto frontier through recursive harness selfimprovement. On Terminal-Bench 2, each round of evolution improves the retained Pareto frontier, yielding higher pass rates at lower costs. For example, the pass rate of the heavy mode rises from 74.6% in epoch 1 to mean of 80.8% in epoch 3, while mean cost per task falls from $0.91 to $0.72. The lite and medium modes also maintain their pass rates from epoch 2 to 3, while their mean costs fall from $0.61 to $0.43 and from $0.68 to $0.56, respectively. The benefits of additional evolution epochs are particularly clear on SWE-Bench Pro, where single run may raise pass rate at the expense of higher cost. In the medium mode, pass rate rises from 70.0% in epoch 1 to 77.0% in epoch 2, but mean cost also rises from $1.57 to $1.66. Only in epoch 3 does it improve both metrics, with pass rate rising to 79.0% and mean cost falling to $1.26 per task. On ProgramBench, the fourth epoch likewise lowers costs across all three modes while maintaining similar pass rates. These patterns highlight an advantage of recursive self-improvement over single-round evolution.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced HARNESSPRO, label-free approach to recursive harness self-improvement that improves task performance while reducing execution cost. To this end, it coordinates trajectory diagnosis and harness modification through multi-agent framework, with dedicated planner proposing update plans and LLM-generated tests guiding candidate evaluation. Rather than producing single harness, HARNESSPRO offers cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) alternatives to meet different deployment budgets. Experiments across three benchmarks show that HARNESSPRO can improve task performance while reducing execution cost, with additional benefits in latency. Further analysis attributes these gains to the synergy of multiple evolved mechanisms and shows sustained progress through recursive self-improvement. These findings show that performance and efficiency can improve together, making cost-aware evolution promising direction for practical recursive self-improvement in harness optimization.

sections.title: B EVOLUTION INSTRUCTIONS
sections.content: Listing 1 Cost-focused evolution instruction (I1) Prioritize reducing average execution cost while preserving task correctness and reliable completion. Seek genuine efficiency gains, not lower bills obtained by skipping required work, abandoning difficult tasks, or weakening validation. Use the diagnostics, trajectories, and candidate implementations to distinguish necessary work from avoidable expense. Look for recurring sources of redundant exploration, repeated context, or lowvalue verification. Consider the total cost of execution, including unsuccessful attempts and any overhead introduced by the proposed change; fewer steps or shorter outputs alone do not establish an improvement. Possible directions include adapting reasoning effort to individual public tasks, managing context and tool feedback economically, and improving convergence or recovery. Preserve the information and checks needed for dependable results. These are optional search directions, not checklist: derive any mechanism from the available evidence, without assuming routing rubric, fixed thresholds, profile taxonomy, or pertask rules. Propose focused, generalizable plan rather than accumulating optimizations. Explain which observed expense each change addresses, why correctness should be preserved, and what regression risks remain. Distinguish expected savings from measured results; the fixed external evaluator, not the plans claims, determines whether quality is maintained and cost is reduced. Listing 2 Balanced evolution instruction (I2) Seek balanced improvement in task reliability and average execution cost. Treat correctness and efficiency as joint objectives: do not pursue savings by neglecting required behavior, or assume that additional computation necessarily improves quality. balanced plan should improve the tradeoff, not simply average the other directions. Use the diagnostics, trajectories, and candidate implementations to identify where effort contributes to successful completion and where it is redundant. Compare peer candidates to understand their strengths, weaknesses, and interactions, rather than copying their mechanisms wholesale. Prefer changes that remove lowvalue work while preserving or strengthening the reasoning and validation that matter. Possible directions include taskadaptive reasoning effort, concise but recoverable context, effective use of tool feedback, and verification or recovery guided by observed uncertainty. These are optional hypotheses, not prescribed designs. Infer an appropriate approach from the evidence; no routing rubric, fixed thresholds, profile names, or pertask rules are supplied. Account for the overhead and complexity of combining changes. Propose coherent, generalizable plan and explain its expected quality and cost effects together. Make uncertain tradeoffs and regression risks explicit, including why any added work is worthwhile. Keep predicted benefits separate from established findings and let the fixed external evaluator determine whether the joint improvement is real.

Focus on reliable completion and correct behavior, not more elaborate execution for its own sake. Performancefocused evolution should invest effort where it can address meaningful failures, rather than increase computation uniformly across tasks. Use the diagnostics, trajectories, and candidate implementations to identify consequential failure patterns and the limitations behind them. Examine both successful and unsuccessful executions to distinguish useful reasoning or validation from activity that merely adds cost. Draw on peer candidates when their behavior provides relevant evidence, but do not assume that more complex harness is more capable one. Possible directions include adapting reasoning effort to the public task, selective deeper investigation or independent verification, and stronger context or recovery management. These are optional hypotheses, not an implementation recipe. Derive the actual design from evidence; no routing rubric, fixed thresholds, mandatory review schedule, or pertask rules are supplied. Preserve efficient behavior where additional work has no demonstrated purpose. Propose focused, generalizable plan that explains which failures it aims to prevent and why the changes should help. If additional work is necessary, state the expected quality benefit, cost implications, and remaining risks without presenting predictions as measured gains. The fixed external evaluator determines whether the improvement justifies the resulting qualitycost tradeoff.

It supplements the benchmark rules; it never permits source retrieval, internet access, decompilation, tracing, or reuse of the reference executable. ## Evidencefirst workflow 1. Read all bundled documentation and turn it into compact behavior ledger: commands, flags, inputs, outputs, exit status, file effects, defaults, error behavior, formatting, and explicitly documented edge cases. 2. Establish runnable skeleton early. Create compile.sh, build minimal independent executable, and confirm the complete build/run cycle before investing in secondary behavior. 3. Probe the reference through its normal public interface. Use small, discriminating experiments that separate plausible behaviors; record the observed input, output, status, and state change instead of relying on assumptions based on the program name. 4. Prioritize breadth before polish. Implement the documented happy paths and common input classes, then error handling, boundary cases, formatting, and lowfrequency options. Keep list of remaining unsupported behavior. 5. Compare your implementation and the reference on the same locally generated cases. When they differ, reduce the case and fix the underlying general rule rather than adding oneoff special case. 6. Rebuild from clean state periodically. solution that works only because of cached artifacts, undeclared tools, or files outside the submission is not complete. 7. Before finalizing, verify that compile.sh is executable, produces ./executable without network access, and that representative success and failure probes agree with the reference. ## Efficiency rules Batch independent documentation reads and related probes when practical. Prefer highinformation probes over broad random exploration. Keep outputs bounded and summarize findings in the behavior ledger. Stop repeating probes once stable rule has been established. Reserve the final portion of the budget for clean rebuild and endtoend validation rather than continued exploration. ## Reference lifecycle Keep the blackbox reference available until differential validation is finished. Develop separately built candidate at another path, with the same executable basename where relevant. Do not overwrite the reference during implementation. If permitted move is necessary, retain the executeonly reference on the same filesystem without reading/copying its bytes or changing its permissions. The reference is only development oracle: never include it in the submission or invoke it from the submitted implementation. Selfauthored expected outputs
